{{Short description|Property of a product of terms that collapses via cancellation}}
In [[mathematics]], a '''[[Telescoping (mathematics)|telescoping]] [[Product (mathematics)|product]]''' is a product of a sequence of factors that simplifies dramatically because most intermediate terms cancel, leaving only the initial and final terms. This phenomenon is closely related to the concept of a [[Telescoping series|telescoping sum]], but applies to multiplicative structures instead of additive ones. It is also known as a '''method of quotients''' due to its interpretation as repeated division of successive terms.<ref name=":0">{{cite web|language=en |title=Telescoping Product |url=https://brilliant.org/wiki/telescoping-series-product/ |website=brilliant.org}}<!-- auto-translated from Polish by Module:CS1 translator --></ref>

== Definition ==
Let <math>A \subseteq \mathbb{Z}</math> and let <math>g : A \to \mathbb{R}</math> be a function such that <math>g(n) \neq 0</math> for all relevant <math>n</math>.

A sequence <math>f(n)</math> is said to define a '''telescoping product''' if it can be written in the form

: <math>f(n) = \frac{g(n+1)}{g(n)}.</math>

Then the finite product

: <math>\prod_{k=m}^{n} f(k)</math>

collapses as intermediate terms cancel.<ref name=":0" />

This is why the telescoping product is often referred to as the '''method of quotients''': each factor represents a quotient of successive values of a function.

== Fundamental identity ==
If <math>g(k) \neq 0</math> for all <math>k</math>, then:

: <math>\prod_{k=m}^{n} \frac{g(k+1)}{g(k)} = \frac{g(n+1)}{g(m)}.</math>

All intermediate terms cancel pairwise, leaving only the boundary terms.

== Interpretation ==
The telescoping product can be viewed as the multiplicative analogue of the finite difference method used in telescoping sums. While sums use differences <math>g(n+1)-g(n)</math>, products use ratios <math>g(n+1)/g(n)</math>. In both cases, the structure ensures that intermediate contributions vanish in the final expression.<ref name=":0" />

== Examples ==

=== Basic example ===
Let

: <math>f(n) = \frac{n+1}{n}.</math>

Then

: <math>\prod_{k=1}^{n} \frac{k+1}{k}

 = \frac{2}{1} \cdot \frac{3}{2} \cdot \frac{4}{3} \cdots \frac{n+1}{n}

 = n+1.</math>

All intermediate factors cancel, leaving only the final numerator and initial denominator.

=== Factorial-related example ===
Let

: <math>f(n) = \frac{n}{n-1} \quad (n \ge 2).</math>

Then

: <math>\prod_{k=2}^{n} \frac{k}{k-1}

 = \frac{n}{1} = n.</math>

This is another direct consequence of successive cancellation.

=== Example using a general sequence ===
For any sequence <math>g(n)</math> with nonzero terms:

: <math>\frac{g(2)}{g(1)} \cdot \frac{g(3)}{g(2)} \cdot \frac{g(4)}{g(3)} \cdots \frac{g(n+1)}{g(n)}

 = \frac{g(n+1)}{g(1)}.</math>

== Relation to telescoping sums ==
Telescoping products are the multiplicative analogue of telescoping sums. In additive form:

: <math>\sum (g(n+1) - g(n)) = g(n+1) - g(m).</math>

In multiplicative form:

: <math>\prod \frac{g(n+1)}{g(n)} = \frac{g(n+1)}{g(m)}.</math>

Both rely on the same cancellation principle, but operate in different algebraic structures.
